summary: For 5–7s, teach the durable frame 'my body needs these things, and it often tells me when it doesn't have them'. The four basic needs — food (energy to move/think/grow), water (hydration), sleep (rest and growth), exercise (strong muscles and heart) — are anchored to bodily feelings the child already knows: hungry, thirsty and sleepy signal that food, water or sleep is needed, while a heart beating faster during and after moving shows the body working when we exercise (it is not a signal that exercise is missing). The key idea is need→consequence as simple cause-and-effect, drawn from the child's own experience rather than abstract categories or nutritional detail. Keep it concrete and personal, and distinguish a need (the body must have it) from a want (sweets, toys we merely enjoy).
misconceptions: 'Food and water are the only needs' — forgetting that sleep and exercise are equally basic needs, not optional extras.
'Only some people/athletes need exercise' — missing that movement is a need for every body.
'Needs are just things I like/want' — not distinguishing a want (sweets, toys) from a need the body requires to work.
'You only need to sleep when you're tired' — missing that sleep is a regular requirement for growth and rest.
'Snacks/juice are the same as meals and water' — an early confusion that anticipates the balanced-diet topic.
'These are human-only needs' — not yet seeing that animals share the same basic needs.

activities.title: Look after a character: meet each need
steps: Care for a character (e.g. 'Ollie') whose four needs — food, water, sleep, exercise — gently drain over time, shown by soft meters and by the character's behaviour (rubbing its tummy, yawning, flopping, getting fidgety).
Choose an action — give a meal, give a drink, tuck into bed for a nap, go for a run — and watch the character perk up when the matching need is met.
Deliberately try a mismatched action (a drink when the character is sleepy, a nap when it is hungry) and notice it does NOT fix that droop.
Say out loud which signal means which need: 'yawning means it needs sleep', 'rubbing tummy means it needs food'.
activities.insight: The body has four distinct needs, and in this game each one has its own signal that only the matching action fixes — a drink won't cure sleepiness, a nap won't cure hunger. (Real bodies are a bit messier: feeling tired can sometimes come from being hungry or thirsty too.)

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal: the body and its needs
steps: Look at a picture of a child and tap different parts to reveal each need: tummy→food, mouth→water, closed eyes→sleep, legs/heart→exercise.
For each, reveal 'why' the body needs it (food for energy, water for hydration, sleep for rest and growth, exercise for strong muscles and heart).
Lift a flap for 'what happens without it?' to connect each need to its consequence (no water→thirsty, no sleep→tired).
activities.insight: Each need is tied to a part of the body and a felt signal, and each matters for a specific reason.

activities.title: Sort needs from wants (and match consequences)
steps: Sort everyday pictures (a bed, a meal, a water bottle, running) into the four needs.
Add a mix of 'want' pictures (sweets, a toy, TV) and decide which are needs the body must have and which are things we simply enjoy.
Match each need to what happens without it ('no sleep → tired', 'no water → thirsty').
Try the heartbeat test: do star jumps, then feel your heart to notice how movement changes the body.
activities.insight: A need is something the body must have to work; a want is something we like but could do without — and movement is a need for every body, not only for athletes.

activities.title: Advise a tired or hungry character (talk it through)
steps: Talk with a puppet or friendly character who says things like 'Why am I so tired?' or 'Why do I feel so thirsty?'
Advise the character which need to meet and say why (what that need does for the body).
Challenge a mistaken character who says 'I don't need exercise, I just need food and sleep' by explaining what exercise does.
activities.insight: Children can reason aloud about which need is unmet and justify it by naming the need's job (e.g. sleep for rest and growth, exercise for strong muscles and heart).

checkQuestion: Your body needs food, water, sleep and exercise. Someone says: 'Sleep is just boring — I'd be totally fine if I never slept, I just wouldn't be bored.' Is that right? What does your body actually use sleep for, and what would happen to you if you didn't get any?
checkAnswer: Sleep is a real body need, not just boredom-filling: the body uses it to rest and to grow. Without enough sleep you feel tired and can't think, move or grow properly. (Each need has a job — food for energy, water for hydration, exercise for strength — and missing any one causes a bodily effect.)
